query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys, exposure to intermediate temperatures combined with low-strain cyclic loading induces nanoclustering of the principal elements (Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni) along grain boundaries. This nanoclustering diminishes grain boundary cohesion and serves as a precursor to intergranular crack initiation, thereby leading to a brittle fracture mode distinct from conventional precipitation-induced embrittlement.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase face-centered cubic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy with uniform distribution of elements and minimal pre-existing grain boundary segregation.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled isothermal thermal aging at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 500–700 °C) combined with low-strain cyclic loading designed to mimic service conditions. Use advanced microscopy (APT and high-resolution TEM) to monitor the evolution of nanoclusters at grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Intermediate aging temperatures (500–700 °C) and mild cyclic mechanical loading. Experimental design includes multiple treatment sets: (i) thermal aging alone, (ii) cyclic loading alone, and (iii) combined aging and cyclic loading, to isolate the contribution of each stimulus.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoclusters of principal elements forming at the grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: At intermediate temperatures, enhanced atomic mobility initiates local diffusion that promotes nanoclustering of the principal elements at grain boundaries. Concurrent cyclic mechanical loading further accentuates this segregation, undermining the cohesive strength of the grain boundaries and leading to premature intergranular fracture.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples experiencing both thermal aging and cyclic loading will exhibit a higher density of GB nanoclusters as characterized by APT and TEM, with a correlated decrease in ductility and an onset of intergranular cracking. Control samples (with either thermal aging or loading alone) should show lower levels of nanoclustering and maintain better toughness.
generation.baseline: An as-cast, minimally treated CrMnFeCoNi HEA exhibiting uniform grain boundary chemistry and ductile, transgranular failure behavior under standard tensile tests.
generation.boundary: This embrittlement mechanism is expected to be significant under intermediate service temperatures (500–700 °C) where atomic mobility permits nanocluster formation. At cryogenic or significantly higher temperatures, other mechanisms (e.g., twinning at low temperatures or dissolution of clusters at very high temperatures) may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: While literature supports that nanoclustering can reduce GB cohesion, the precise threshold of cluster density required to trigger brittle failure in these alloys is not yet established. Furthermore, the quantitative interplay between thermal aging and cyclic loading in promoting nanoclustering remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several sets of CrMnFeCoNi HEA samples: one set subjected solely to thermal aging, one solely to cyclic loading, and one to the combination of both. Use atom probe tomography and high-resolution TEM to quantify the nanocluster density at the grain boundaries. Perform tensile tests to relate observed microstructural changes to macroscopic mechanical properties (ductility and fracture mode).
measurements: Nanocluster density and distribution at GBs (via APT)
Local chemical composition of GBs (via TEM with EDS)
Tensile ductility and fracture mode (via standardized tensile testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples subjected to the combined interventions do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in GB nanocluster density relative to controls, or if the enhanced nanoclustering does not correlate with a measurable decrease in ductility and the emergence of intergranular fracture, then the hypothesis that nanoclustering-induced GB decohesion is the primary mechanism for embrittlement will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs reduces GB cohesion in single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys. AbstractThe loss of ductility with temperature has been widely observed in tensile tests of single-phase face-centered cubic structured high-entropy alloys (HEAs). However, the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss remains unknown. Here, we show that ductility loss in the CrMnFeCoNi HEA upon deformation at intermediate temperatures is correlated with cracking at grain boundaries (GBs). Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to avoid ductility loss by shifting the fast segregation of principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases. We believe that GB decohesion by nanoclustering multiprincipal elements is a common phenomenon in HEAs. This study not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a strategy for tailoring ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.

In addition, the segregation of trace elements C and B into GBs is beneficial to improve GB cohesion as long as M6C carbides do not precipitate (, ). The 1D compositional profiles in fig. S4 show that the C and B composition at Cr-enriched and Ni(Mn)-enriched GBs is very low, which is insufficient to form carbides or borides at GBs. A recent study of the single-phase fcc CoFeNi2V0.5Mo0.2 HEA demonstrated that the lack of Cr and Mn can evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures (). Therefore, we believe that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni system HEAs can embrittle GBs and, hence, lead to ductility loss with increasing deformation temperature. Note that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs also occurs at relatively low temperatures (<700°C), which accounts for ductility loss at intermediate temperatures. In the current work, the sample after tensile test at 700°C, exhibiting remarkable ductility loss though maintaining a strain hardening capacity, provides a good model example to demonstrate our hypothesis: Nanoclustering induced GB embrittlement in HEAs at intermediate temperatures. proposals.intervention: Perform controlled thermal aging with isothermal holds at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 500–700 °C) while applying low-strain cyclic loading, followed by atom probe tomography (APT) and high-resolution TEM to monitor grain boundary compositional evolution.
proposals.conditions: Test samples under controlled atmospheres (inert gas) at intermediate temperatures with varying aging times (e.g., 1–100 hours) combined with mild cyclic mechanical load to simulate service conditions.
proposals.structural_mediator: Nanoclustering and segregation of principal elements (Cr, Ni, and Mn) at grain boundaries.
proposals.mechanism: At intermediate service temperatures, even an initially single-phase HEA may undergo local elemental segregation at GBs which reduces the cohesion by inducing nanoclusters that act as crack nucleation sites. This GB decohesion mechanism contrasts with conventional intergranular precipitation in simpler alloys.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Samples that undergo aging will show increased nanocluster density at grain boundaries correlated with the onset of intergranular cracking and embrittlement, while control samples (with minimal aging or loading) maintain ductility.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It tests a mechanistic hypothesis that brittleness emerges from GB nanoclustering in compositionally complex alloys rather than from traditional precipitate formation or grain coarsening, establishing a controlled comparison against conventional alloy behavior.

proposals.intervention: Apply controlled thermomechanical treatments to obtain two microstructural states: one with significant deformation-induced twins (via low-temperature cold rolling) and one with a fully recrystallized, twin-free microstructure (via high-temperature annealing).
proposals.conditions: Conduct tensile tests at intermediate service temperatures (e.g., 650 °C) and strain rates that mimic engineering service conditions.
proposals.structural_mediator: Deformation twins and modified grain boundary morphology.
proposals.mechanism: The formation of deformation twins in the cold-worked sample leads to local strain localization at twin–grain boundary intersections, which reduces effective grain boundary cohesion and promotes brittle-like fracture. In contrast, the recrystallized, twin-free state should maintain higher toughness.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Under identical tensile loading, the cold-worked, twinned microstructure will exhibit a lower ductility and earlier onset of intergranular fracture compared to the recrystallized sample. This controlled comparison distinguishes the GB-related embrittlement mechanism in HEAs from conventional ductile-to-brittle transitions.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By directly correlating microstructural twin formation with brittle behavior, this approach elucidates whether and how deformation-induced features in a single-phase, compositionally complex alloy contribute to toughness degradation.

proposals.intervention: Introduce controlled amounts of interstitial impurities (oxygen/nitrogen) during melting, then subject samples to aging treatments at high service temperatures (around 700 °C) under vacuum or controlled gas atmospheres.
proposals.conditions: Expose samples to isothermal aging for variable durations (e.g., 10–100 hours) at 700 °C while monitoring impurity diffusion and potential phase segregation using nanoindentation and microscopy.
proposals.structural_mediator: Interstitial impurity segregation leading to local matrix depletion and potential incipient phase segregation at grain boundaries.
proposals.mechanism: Even in an initially single-phase refractory HEA, impurity elements such as oxygen and nitrogen promote the local depletion of solid solution strengthening components near grain boundaries. This results in a weakened GB region and a propensity for brittle intergranular fracture under service loading.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Samples with elevated controlled impurity levels will exhibit a measurable decrease in hardness and toughness, especially after prolonged aging. A decisive falsification outcome would be the absence of any GB segregated impurities and no corresponding reduction in ductility compared to ultra-pure control samples.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It provides a testable hypothesis that brittleness in complex alloys can arise from impurity-driven phase segregation at GBs, distinct from the traditional precipitate-driven embrittlement seen in conventional alloys.

proposals.intervention: Perform in situ high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) tensile tests under ultra-high vacuum while systematically varying strain rate and temperature to examine dynamic microstructural evolution, particularly in the grain boundary regions.
proposals.conditions: Test under a range of strain rates (from 10⁻³ to 10² s⁻¹) and temperatures (cryogenic to room temperature) to capture the threshold conditions for dynamic amorphization at grain boundaries.
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline, dynamically amorphized layer at grain boundaries during high-strain-rate deformation.
proposals.mechanism: Upon rapid deformation, local adiabatic heating and severe plastic strain may cause transient amorphization of the grain boundary regions. This nanocrystalline, amorphous layer lacks the typical ductile absorption mechanisms, leading to brittle fracture initiation at GBs—a phenomenon distinct from coventional alloy embrittlement governed by static precipitate formation.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Above a critical strain rate and specific temperature range, in situ TEM will reveal the onset of dynamic amorphization limited to the GBs, coinciding with a reduction in toughness. Failure would occur predominantly along these amorphous interfaces. A decisive falsification outcome would be the absence of any dynamic GB amorphization despite similar deformation conditions.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach tests a novel mechanism—dynamic, strain-induced amorphization of grain boundaries—as the cause of toughness degradation in a single-phase HEA, differentiating it fundamentally from conventional precipitation or grain-coarsening mechanisms.

critiques.addresses_problem: The hypothesis directly tackles the open question by proposing that dynamic, strain-induced amorphization localized at the grain boundaries causes the embrittlement, rather than conventional static precipitate formation.
critiques.constraints: It respects the constraint of maintaining a compositionally complex, single-phase CoCrFeMnNi alloy and targets a deformation regime where rapid strain rates and controlled temperatures are used.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism, based on local adiabatic heating and severe plastic strain triggering transient amorphization of the grain boundary regions, is plausible; however, the manifestation of dynamic amorphization in a fcc HEA (as opposed to reported examples in other contexts) remains to be definitively established.
critiques.feasibility: In situ HRTEM tensile tests under ultra-high vacuum over the specified strain rates and temperatures are within the realm of established methods, although technically challenging.
critiques.evidence: Records (PMC7311485 and PMC12463061) mention dynamic amorphization in different alloy systems and the importance of strain‐hardening behavior under dynamic conditions. However, none of the records directly show this mechanism in CoCrFeMnNi alloys.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is that dynamic amorphization might not actually develop in the grain boundaries of fcc CoCrFeMnNi HEAs under the test conditions, making the observed embrittlement possibly attributable to other mechanisms.
critiques.fix: Include complementary diagnostics (e.g., local temperature mapping or additional spectroscopy) to verify that any observed amorphous layers are indeed due to dynamic deformation rather than other transient microstructural changes.

critiques.addresses_problem: This approach attempts to address toughness degradation by correlating deformation-induced twins with a reduction in effective grain boundary cohesion, offering a mechanism distinct from conventional precipitation.
critiques.constraints: It meets the constraint by working with an Al0.3CoCrFeNi HEA and by designing a controlled comparison between a twinned, cold-rolled state and a twin-free recrystallized state under service-relevant conditions.
critiques.physical_soundness: While twin formation can lead to local strain localization, the direct link between twins and GB embrittlement in a compositionally complex alloy is less well established than for other mechanisms; the hypothesis might oversimplify the interplay of strengthening and ductility.
critiques.feasibility: The required thermomechanical treatments are standard, and tensile testing at the prescribed conditions is feasible; microstructural characterization of twins is also well-developed.
critiques.evidence: The supplied evidence (e.g., PMC8840145) demonstrates that twins can influence mechanical properties, although these studies often report enhanced strength–ductility combinations rather than a direct switch to brittle behavior.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that deformation-induced twins in the HEA may not actually reduce grain boundary cohesion enough to cause brittle failure; instead, they may contribute to strain hardening and toughness.
critiques.fix: Clarify the conditions under which twin-induced strain localization transforms from beneficial strengthening to detrimental embrittlement, and include direct measurements of GB cohesion (such as local fracture analyses) to strengthen the hypothesis.

critiques.addresses_problem: This hypothesis explains embrittlement as arising from impurity-driven segregation at grain boundaries leading to local matrix depletion, a mechanism that is distinct from classical intermetallic precipitation seen in conventional alloys.
critiques.constraints: It adheres to the constraint by using a refractory HEA (e.g., TiVNbTa) designed for demanding engineering applications, although care must be taken that the impurity levels remain controlled.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically sound, as impurities like oxygen and nitrogen are known to promote local phase segregation and weaken boundary cohesion, as supported by CALPHAD and nanoindentation studies in the literature.
critiques.feasibility: Controlled introduction of interstitial impurities during alloy melting, followed by thermal aging and standard characterization methods, is feasible with current experimental capabilities.
critiques.evidence: Evidence from PMC10708198 supports the impurity-induced phase segregation mechanism and its effect on softening, although the emphasis there is on softening rather than a direct brittle fracture; the extension to embrittlement is a reasonable hypothesis.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that the impurity levels required to trigger significant GB segregation may be difficult to control or might introduce additional effects (e.g., overall softening rather than brittle failure) that confound interpretation.
critiques.fix: Establish a tight quantitative control of impurity concentrations and perform complementary fracture analyses to confirm that the impurity-induced segregation leads to embrittlement rather than just softening.

critiques.addresses_problem: This mechanism directly targets the question by proposing that nanoclustering of principal elements at the grain boundaries, causing GB decohesion, is responsible for brittleness in an ostensibly single-phase HEA.
critiques.constraints: It respects all constraints by working with a single-phase CrMnFeCoNi HEA and testing under conditions (intermediate temperatures and controlled cyclic loading) relevant to service conditions.
critiques.physical_soundness: The proposed mechanism is physically well grounded; atom probe tomography and high-resolution TEM studies have clearly shown nanoclustering-induced GB embrittlement in similar HEA systems.
critiques.feasibility: The combination of controlled thermal aging, cyclic loading, and state-of-the-art microstructural analysis (APT and TEM) is well within established experimental methodologies.
critiques.evidence: Multiple records (e.g., PMC6897545, records in PMC6897545 for nanoclustering and GB embrittlement) strongly support the occurrence of nanoclustering at GBs and its detrimental effect on ductility.
critiques.main_risk: The chief risk lies in clearly attributing the embrittlement to nanoclustering rather than other concurrent microstructural evolutions, and in ensuring that the cyclic loading does not inadvertently trigger additional recovery processes.
critiques.fix: Incorporate a systematic control experiment to separate the effects of thermal aging and mechanical cyclic loading, ensuring that the observed nanoclustering is solely correlated with embrittlement.

decision.rationale: Direction D directly addresses the open question by proposing that, even in a single-phase high-entropy alloy, nanoclustering of principal elements at the grain boundaries leads to reduced cohesion and eventual brittle failure. This mechanism is well supported by previous atom probe tomography and TEM studies (e.g., evidence from PMC6897545) and distinguishes the embrittlement behavior from conventional coarse-scale precipitation or grain coarsening. Although cyclic loading and thermal aging are both used to stimulate nanoclustering, a systematic control experiment is needed to isolate the effects of each factor, a fix that strengthens the approach without departing from the original proposal.
